name: February 1986 Storm

phenomena.details: Significant storm with Dst ~ −312 nT, notably occurring during solar minimum between cycles 21 and 22.

impacts.description: HF radio disruptions on polar routes; unexpected given the solar-minimum conditions.
Aurora visible at unusually low latitudes for a solar minimum period; reported from the northern United States and central Europe.

papers.title: Ring current development during the great geomagnetic storm of February 1986
papers.authors: Hamilton, D. C., Gloeckler, G., Ipavich, F. M., et al.
papers.journal: Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics
papers.keyFinding: Analysed the February 1986 storm as a notable example of an intense geomagnetic storm occurring during solar minimum, driven by a coronal hole high-speed stream interaction region.

summary: The February 1986 storm (Dst ~ −312 nT) struck during the deep minimum between Solar Cycles 21 and 22, driven by a coronal mass ejection from a single large active region that erupted repeatedly in early February – a reminder that intense storms can come from isolated regions even when overall activity is low.
description: On February 6–8, 1986, an intense geomagnetic storm drove the Dst index to approximately −312 nT during the solar minimum between Solar Cycles 21 and 22. The driver was not a coronal-hole stream but a fast coronal mass ejection: a single large active region produced a series of major flares between February 4 and 7, and the resulting ejecta reached Earth on February 8 with a sustained southward magnetic field. Hamilton et al. (1988) used the storm to study ring-current development, finding an unusually large contribution from ionospheric oxygen ions at storm peak. The event surprised forecasters and remains an important case study: it showed that infrastructure must be prepared for severe storms at any phase of the solar cycle, since one energetic active region is sufficient.
